title: “众筹本质上是一场营销与社区运营”——2026 年开发者用 Kickstarter 融资须知
content:
"Crowdfunding is fundamentally a marketing and a community exercise" – What developers need to know about funding a game with Kickstarter in 2026 | GamesIndustry.biz

We might be long past the days of games companies raising eye-watering figures on Kickstarter, but the platform is still a viable way to raise money to fund – at last part of – your game.
Research from Ico Partners' Thomas Bidaux shows
that in 2025, games companies raised $26 million on Kickstarter – level with 2024's figures, and one of the more successful years since the last big Kickstarter boom in 2015.
Research from Ico Partners shows that crowdfunding for games remains steady  |
Image credit:
Ico Partners
Last year, 443 video game projects were successfully funded on Kickstarter, a minor reduction (4%) from 2024's figures. 55 game projects raised over $100,000 in 2025, while 11 made over $500,000.
443 game projects were funded on Kickstarter in 2025  |
Image credit:
Ico Partners
"Last time there were so many $500k-plus projects was in 2015," Bidaux says. "There are early indicators that 2026 will be in line with the 2025 pace. Kickstarter is not funding the whole video games industry, but there are good opportunities for the projects going on the platform."
David Harper, the MD of Skyhook Games, which recently took to Kickstarter to secure funding for
Lawn Mowing Simulator 2
, says that although crowdfunding has never been an easy option, there are different "background challenges" that can have an impact on a project's success.
David Harper  |
Image credit:
Skyhook Games
"Gamers can be paralysed by choice," Harper says. "Marketing channels are flooded, curation is light, and the economy – both within the games industry and more generally – has been pretty tough."
One big challenge facing Kickstarter projects is the barrier to entry. In the platform's early days, companies could simply pitch an idea; Frontier's Elite: Dangerous, for example, was very much a rough and ready work in progress when it raised over £1.5 million on Kickstarter in 2012. Now, you need to have an almost-complete game to secure funding.
"You need to have the game in a state where you can capture release-quality footage, and it is even better if you can offer a demo," Bidaux explains. "Alongside that, you need to be quite advanced in your marketing effort. You need an audience already engaged and interested in the game. The campaign will help reach more people, but you need a starting base to make it work.
"Both of these points mean you cannot turn to Kickstarter on a whim if funds are suddenly scarce, or if you need those funds to make the project presentable.
"Crowdfunding is fundamentally a marketing and a community exercise. In an industry where funding is much more difficult to secure, getting to the point where Kickstarter becomes an option is not easy."
Bad actors
Another challenge faced by Skyhook's Harper is scammers on the Kickstarter platform. Twice, the project received large pledges that "looked great for the campaign", but these accounts were removed. The second instance of this brought the Lawn Mowing Simulator 2 crowdfunding push under its target in the final 24 hours.
The crowdfunding campaign for Lawn Mowing Simulator 2 almost fell at the final hurdle  |
Image credit:
Skyhook Games
"We'd been 'funded' for over three weeks, but the size of the withdrawn pledge meant that we were suddenly back below our campaign target," Harper explains. "Kickstarter kindly offered to extend our campaign by a week, and with support from more backers who saw our situation, we completed the campaign successfully – but the situation made it pretty tough for us to ever really feel in control of our destiny."
Harper admits that this activity is hard for platforms to manage; after all, any additional friction designed to dissuade scammers could also prove problematic for genuine backers.
"The only real way to prevent an experience like ours is to limit the cost of the highest tiers," Harper says. "This prevents a single removed pledge from derailing the campaign overall, but it also limits the opportunity for a genuinely kind soul to support a campaign to that degree. So you just have to balance the risk with the potential reward."
A potentially difficult path
Crowdfunding in the games space is not without its critics. Daniel Milo, indie director at Azoove maker Timeless Toucan,
took to LinkedIn
earlier this year to advise studios not to attempt to fund their games in this manner.
Daniel Milo  |
Image credit:
Daniel Milo
For one, he says that a "mostly finished" game is "almost always" required for success, in addition to an "existing audience". If you are releasing your game on Steam, Milo says that you are "punished" for selling keys via the campaign as the platform ignores "your core audience's reviews". That's on top of an unsuccessful campaign potentially having a negative association that will make it harder to secure a publisher.
"There are plenty of systemic problems with crowdfunding, and due to competitiveness, many studios are forced to engage in tactics I frown upon," Milo continues. "Due to the nature of all-or-nothing funding and the culture of 'funded in 35 seconds', studios are encouraged to place their target drastically below what they actually need to raise, risking a 'funded' game that can't reach the release line."
"Seek traditional funding through publishers, angels, and VCs, if you are desperate"
Milo says that those considering crowdfunding should look at alternatives. The first is the "more traditional path".
"Seek traditional funding through publishers, angels, and VCs, if you are desperate," he says. "If you have a game of sufficient quality and ability to create a marketing campaign that would result in a successful campaign, you have the resources to show traction and quality to the investors."
